title: Jean Goldkette, Don Redman and how the Cotton Pickers got their name
summary: Goldkette hired the band for the Graystone in Detroit and brought in Redman; Jackson praises Redman as an early dance-band arranger and explains the Cotton Pickers name and Victor contract.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: No, he was just the manager. And as the story goes with that band, they used to go up to Manitou Beach, Michigan, every summer to [Clark's Lake] and play. When Jean Goldkette Gene Galkit heard the band up there he liked what he heard, so he was getting ready to build this million dollar ballroom called the Graystone in Detroit. So he liked the band, so he figured with himself that he could do something with this band, so he sent and got Don Redmon to come, and Don Redmon at that time was playing with Fletcher Henderson and, also, Don, back in 1925 and '26, had wrote worked for Jean Goldkette's Gene Galkit's
-- you see. He was one of the forerunners of big band dance arranging. That was before Fletcher Henderson and all those guys.
And it seems as if Fletcher Henderson is given more credit for that than Don.
I know but Don was writing for Fletcher before Fletcher was writing himself.
If you listen to the original arrangement of 'Sugarfoot Stomp,' that's Don Redmon. 'Bean Koo Jack' and all those things, Don Redmon made those arrangements, you see.
You know. But Don was, he was the type of guy, he was a very quiet guy, and so nobody really got to know about him. They've never exploited him to that extent.

McKinney kept him in the background, in a way. Jean Goldkette So Gene Colkit sent him, sent and got him, Fletcher, to come to Detroit and he took this band and he augmented the band and made it 11 pieces and the band sounded so nice and,
I guess, well, being a black band, too, if you listen to it on the air, you couldn't tell whether it was a black band or white band, in a way. So they --
That's right, and so they nicknamed it Cottonpickers, so they'd really know that it was a black band.
Yeah, but that's beautiful. Well, let's go on now. We'll find out what Butter is and everything.
You can carry that on if you want to from there. I'll get back to --

So going back to McKinney Cottonpickers, that turned out to be one of the greatest dance bands in the country at that time. It had the reputation. And Gene Goldkette also got them a contract to record for Victor. I think it was one of the first colored bands to record for Victor, you know.
